supplementary_news.content: เว็บไซต์นี้เก็บข้อมูลคุกกี้ในคอมพิวเตอร์ของคุณ คุกกี้เหล่านี้จะใช้ในการเก็บข้อมูลเกี่ยวกับวิธีที่คุณปฏิสัมพันธ์กับเว็บไซต์ของเรา และอนุญาตให้เราจดจําคุณ เราใช้ข้อมูลนี้เพื่อปรับปรุงและปรับประสบการณ์การเรียกดูเว็บ และเพื่อทําการวิเคราะห์และใช้เกณฑ์การวัดผู้เยี่ยมชมของเราทั้งบนเว็บไซต์นี้และสื่อช่องทางอื่นๆ หากต้องการดูข้อมูลเพิ่มเติมเกี่ยวกับคุกกี้ที่เราใช้ โปรดดูนโยบายความเป็นส่วนตัวของเรา หากคุณปฏิเสธ จะไม่มีการติดตามข้อมูลของคุณเมื่อเข้าเยี่ยมชมเว็บไซต์นี้ จะมีการใช้คุกกี้เดียวในเบราว์เซอร์ของคุณเพื่อจดจําว่าจะไม่มีการติดตามการตั้งค่าหรือความชอบของคุณ การตั้งค่าคุกกี้ ยอมรับทั้งหมด ปฏิเสธ Find a Doctor Appointment Medical Centers Packages 1270 Become a Member EN Home > Health Articles > Liver Cancer: A Common Cause of Death in Thai People – Know Before the Danger Health Articles Knowledge Liver Cancer: A Common Cause of Death in Thai People – Know Before the Danger RAPEEPUN KALAYAVINAI, M.D. According to data from the Ministry of Public Health, “liver cancer” is the leading cause of death among Thai people. Meanwhile, information from the World Cancer Research Fund indicates that in 2022, Thailand had the fourth highest liver cancer mortality rate in the world. The major issue is that most patients are usually diagnosed at the late stage and cannot be completely cured. Therefore, liver cancer screening is extremely important, because if detected at an early stage, it can increase the chances of complete treatment or at least improve the patient’s quality of life and longevity. Key Takeaways Liver cancer is a common type of cancer and is the leading cause of death among Thai people. Risk factors that may cause liver cancer include hepatitis B and C virus infection, cirrhosis, fatty liver disease, alcohol consumption, smoking, or exposure to Aflatoxin. Early-stage liver cancer usually does not show symptoms, causing many patients to be diagnosed at an advanced stage, which makes treatment more difficult. Annual health check-ups and hepatitis B vaccination help reduce the risk of liver cancer. Early detection increases the chances of complete treatment and maintaining quality of life. Understanding ‘Liver Cancer’: The Silent Danger Number One That Thai People Should Be Careful Of Liver cancer, or Hepatocellular Carcinoma, is cancer that occurs in the liver, caused by liver cells that undergo mutations and divide continuously without control. These cells multiply to form malignant tumors in the liver and can spread to other organs in the body. In Thailand, liver cancer is one of the most common cancers and is a leading cause of death, particularly in men, who are much more likely to develop the disease than women. The danger of the disease usually lies in late detection, so when diagnosed, many patients are already in the advanced stage, which is difficult to cure. What Causes Liver Cancer? Normal cells in the body have a process to control cell growth. However, mutated cells lose this control and divide abnormally, forming malignant tumors that can invade or spread to other organs. Several factors can lead to liver cancer, as follows: Chronic hepatitis B and C virus infection, a major cause commonly found in Thailand. Cirrhosis from various causes, such as regular alcohol consumption or liver damage from autoimmune disorders. Fatty liver disease, especially in cases of obesity, diabetes, or high blood lipid levels. Smoking. Exposure to certain toxins, such as Aflatoxin in fungi. Genetics. Male sex. Symptoms of Liver Cancer: Watch Early Before It’s Too Late Liver cancer is dangerous because, in the early stage, patients often show no abnormal symptoms or do not notice them, especially those who already have liver disease. As the disease progresses, liver cancer patients may experience the following symptoms: Fluid in the abdomen or abdominal enlargement Fullness, abdominal pain, or bloating Palpable mass in the abdomen Dark urine Weight loss, loss of appetite, fatigue, weakness Diarrhea or black stools Numbness or cramps in hands and feet Low blood sugar, sweating, fainting Skin or muscle inflammation Jaundice, itching Bone pain Internal bleeding, anemia Who is at Risk for Liver Cancer? Those at risk for liver cancer include: Individuals with relatives who have liver disease or family history of liver cancer Individuals with chronic hepatitis B or C Individuals with iron overload in the liver (Hemochromatosis) Individuals with genetic disorders such as Tyrosinemia Individuals with cirrhosis Individuals exposed to Aflatoxin from fungi, commonly found in stored crushed peanuts or old chili powder Individuals with liver inflammation due to fatty liver disease Diagnosis of Liver Cancer Whether showing abnormal symptoms or at risk for liver cancer, screening and diagnosis should be performed using the following methods: Medical history and physical examination by a physician Blood tests to assess liver function, measure liver cancer marker Alpha-Fetoprotein (AFP), and detect hepatitis viruses Radiological examinations such as ultrasound, CT scan, or MRI Biopsy for cancer examination Treatment Options for Liver Cancer Treatment depends on the severity or stage of the disease and the patient’s overall condition. Doctors often use multiple methods together to control the spread of cancer cells, as follows: Hepatic Resection Partial liver resection is the most effective liver cancer treatment, offering higher chances of complete cure compared to other methods. It is suitable for early-stage patients with small tumors that have not spread, normal liver function, and overall good health. Thermal Ablation Thermal ablation destroys liver cancer cells using heat. It is suitable for early-stage patients with small tumors. The treatment results are nearly comparable to liver surgery, but recurrence risk is slightly higher. It is an option for patients with impaired liver function or poor overall health unsuitable for surgery. Liver Transplantation Liver transplantation involves removing the diseased liver and replacing it with a new one. Limitations include finding a matching donor liver, risk of organ rejection, and lifelong immunosuppressive drugs affecting long-term immunity. It is used for patients with non-metastatic liver cancer and concurrent cirrhosis. Transarterial Chemoembolization (TACE) TACE delivers chemotherapy directly to the tumor or its supplying blood vessel while blocking blood flow, causing the tumor to die. It is chosen when liver cancer has begun to spread or surgery is not feasible due to tumor location near large vessels, cirrhosis, or high surgical risk. Systemic Chemotherapy Systemic chemotherapy, including targeted therapy or immunotherapy, specifically attacks cancer cells to destroy or inhibit their division. It is available in injectable and oral forms. Radiotherapy Radiotherapy destroys liver cancer cells using focused radiation, without affecting surrounding organs or causing side effects. Palliative Care Palliative care does not aim to cure the disease but alleviates pain from liver cancer, improving the patient’s quality of life. Can Liver Cancer Be Prevented? Liver cancer arises from multiple factors but can be prevented by maintaining health and avoiding risk behaviors: Avoid alcohol and smoking Be cautious with foods potentially contaminated with Aflatoxin, such as peanuts, dried chili, or moldy onions Control diet, reduce high-fat and high-starch foods Exercise regularly Avoid hepatitis virus infection, do not share personal items, and receive hepatitis vaccination Undergo liver cancer screening, especially for high-risk groups such as those with cirrhosis, hepatitis virus infection, or family history of liver cancer Liver Cancer: Early Awareness Increases Chances of Cure Liver cancer is common and has a high mortality rate because most cases are detected at an advanced stage. However, good hygiene, regular annual health check-ups, and hepatitis B vaccination can reduce risk. Early detection and timely treatment provide a chance for complete cure and the restoration of a good quality of life. supplementary_news.content: British pharmaceutical company GSK is turning to patient data gathered from the 88 million residents of the Greater Bay Area’s 11 cities to speed up drug development in vaccines and cancer care, as officials push for closer cross-border medical cooperation . GSK Hong Kong and Macau general manager Nicholas Teo said patient data was very important because it could form “supplementary evidence” to support regulatory filings and potential label expansions, and also help to “discover benefits other than the medication itself”. Vaccines were one example, Teo said last week. While their effectiveness against target diseases such as flu, shingles and respiratory syncytial virus was well established, he said researchers were increasingly studying potential benefits relating to cardiovascular health and neurological outcomes, which might help generate additional evidence and insights for future healthcare decision-making. Teo said GSK’s expertise lay in vaccination and disease prevention, citing shingles and respiratory syncytial virus as key areas, with the viral liver infection hepatitis B another area of focus. He added that GSK also had a growing oncology and haematology portfolio. View in App READ FULL ARTICLE The bay area is a government scheme aimed at integrating Hong Kong, Macau and nine cities in mainland China’s Guangdong province into a single economic and business hub. Their combined gross domestic product last year was more than US$2.23 trillion, according to official data. GSK signed a memorandum of understanding in September last year with the University of Hong Kong and the Greater Bay Area International Clinical Trial Institute on a study to examine the long-term health effects of the shingles vaccine. Teo said GSK would provide financial sponsorship for the HKU-led study and was also investing in shared data infrastructure. The company could access patient data through the partnership, such as data coming from hospitals and government agencies, but pharmaceutical companies did not have direct access to it on their own, he added. The institute, based in the Hetao Shenzhen-Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone and set up by the Hong Kong government, enables the free exchange of researchers and data between the two cities. Better decisions are made after we have better data Nicholas Teo, GSK Hong Kong and Macau He said real-world data was patient data gathered during routine clinical practice at hospitals and clinics. HKU pharmacy professor Ian Wong said at the conference that cross-border research required “infrastructure that’s safe enough” as the first pillar, alongside government regulation, ethics and public education, before real-world data could be used effectively. Raphael Yeung, a senior pharmacist at Hong Kong’s Drug Office, said the city had multiple regulatory safeguards in place, including the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance. Teo said the value of data ultimately came down to better outcomes and better policy. “Better decisions are made after we have better data,” he said. “If we have data that tells you a certain medication or vaccine benefits a particular population, the government can take a decision on whether to make it available, subsidise it, or improve access.” Teo added that GSK wanted to help prove that the cross-border data pipeline could work at scale. “We hope to be part of potential pilot studies or collaborations that will prove this data flow is safe, secure and high quality between Hong Kong and mainland China,” he said

supplementary_news.content_title: Plasma Cystatin C as a Marker of Acute-on-Chronic Liver Failure and 28-Day Mortality in Patients With Acutely Decompensated Liver Cirrhosis: A Prospective Observational Study
supplementary_news.content: Abstract Background: Acute decompensation of cirrhosis carries a 28-day mortality of 1.9%, rising to nearly 30% with acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF), in which renal failure is the most frequent and most ominous organ failure. Serum creatinine overestimates glomerular filtration rate in cirrhosis. Plasma cystatin C may better reflect renal function and prognosis, but Indian data are scarce. We assessed cystatin C as a marker of ACLF and 28-day mortality in acutely decompensated cirrhosis. Methods: In this prospective observational cohort study, 100 adults with acutely decompensated cirrhosis were enrolled over 18 months. We performed clinical assessments and standard investigations, and measured plasma cystatin C by nephelometric immunoassay within 48 hours of admission. Participants were followed for ACLF and 28-day mortality. Cystatin C, Child-Turcotte-Pugh (CTP), and Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) scores were compared as predictors of mortality by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Results: ACLF developed in 41 participants (41%), and 44 (44%) died within 28 days. Mean plasma cystatin C was higher in non-survivors than survivors (5.49±4.70 vs 2.06±1.54 mg/L; p<0.001) but did not differ by ACLF status (p=0.271). Cystatin C predicted 28-day mortality with AUROC 0.781 (95% CI 0.688-0.874); a cut-off ≥2.5 mg/L gave 73% sensitivity and 75% specificity, outperforming CTP (0.506) and MELD (0.508) scores (p<0.001). Conclusions: Plasma cystatin C rose in patients who died within 28 days and predicted short-term mortality better than CTP or MELD scores, although it did not discriminate ACLF status. Cystatin C may serve as a simple, reproducible adjunct for prognostication in decompensated cirrhosis; larger multicentric studies are needed to validate this cut-off. Introduction Cirrhosis typically evolves from a silent, compensated stage into a decompensated one, announced by ascites, variceal haemorrhage, hepatic encephalopathy or jaundice. Most patients who decompensate acutely still have a reasonably favourable short-term outlook, with roughly 1.9% dying within 28 days; that figure climbs to almost 30% once acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) sets in [1]. Renal failure is the most common organ failure in ACLF and is associated with a worse prognosis than the failure of any other single organ [2]. Serum creatinine remains the most widely used marker of renal function because it is inexpensive and easily available, but its concentration is confounded by reduced muscle mass, low dietary protein intake and increased tubular secretion in cirrhosis, so that it systematically overestimates the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in this population [3,4]. Cystatin C, a low-molecular-weight cysteine-protease inhibitor produced by all nucleated cells at a constant rate and cleared almost exclusively by glomerular filtration, is a more sensitive marker of change in GFR than creatinine and correlates better with directly measured (inulin) clearance in patients with liver cirrhosis [5,6]. It rises within 12 to 24 hours of renal injury, earlier than creatinine, and is less influenced by muscle mass, diet, and bilirubin levels. In a large prospective European cohort, baseline plasma cystatin C independently predicted renal dysfunction, hepatorenal syndrome, ACLF and mortality in patients with acute decompensation of cirrhosis [7]. Data on plasma cystatin C in Indian patients with acutely decompensated cirrhosis are, however, scarce. The primary objective of this study was to assess plasma cystatin C as a predictor of 28-day mortality in patients with acute decompensation of cirrhosis, including its performance relative to the Child-Turcotte-Pugh (CTP) and Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) scores. The secondary objective was to determine whether cystatin C level was associated with the development of ACLF. Note: Cystatin C was not evaluated and is not proposed here as a diagnostic test for ACLF itself. Materials & Methods This prospective, hospital-based observational cohort study was conducted over 18 months in the Department of General Medicine of a tertiary-care teaching hospital in New Delhi, India, along with the Department of Pathology. The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of Vardhman Mahavir Medical College & Safdarjung Hospital (approval no. IEC/VMMC/SJH/Thesis/2019-10/55). Every participant gave written informed consent before enrolment. We screened consecutive adults (aged over 18 years) admitted for acute decompensation of cirrhosis, identified by new-onset or worsening ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, or gastrointestinal bleeding in someone with known cirrhosis, and excluded anyone with pre-existing renal disease or malignancy. All patients meeting these criteria during the enrolment period were included consecutively. None were excluded for missing data. A total of 100 participants completed the 28-day follow-up. The sample size was calculated from a prior report of cystatin C's diagnostic performance (73.3% sensitivity and 52.5% specificity for short-term mortality; 58.0% sensitivity and 66.4% specificity for ACLF) [7] at 80% power, a two-sided α of 0.05 and 15% allowable precision. This required at least 84 participants, so we enrolled 100 to build in a margin. Every participant had a detailed history and examination, abdominal ultrasonography, and venous blood drawn within 48 hours of admission for a complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, serum electrolytes, random blood glucose, viral markers (HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV), and plasma cystatin C. Cystatin C was quantified by particle-enhanced immunonephelometry on a BN II System analyser (Siemens Healthineers, Forchheim, DEU) using a 2 mL ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) sample per the manufacturer's assay protocol. Fasting was not required as cystatin C production and clearance are not materially affected by recent food intake. The GFR was estimated from the 2012 Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) equation that combines creatinine and cystatin C [8]. We applied the Asian Pacific Association for the Study of the Liver (APASL) consensus definition of ACLF, i.e., an acute hepatic insult presenting with jaundice (serum bilirubin above 5 mg/dL) and coagulopathy (international normalised ratio (INR) above 1.5), progressing to ascites and/or hepatic encephalopathy within four weeks in someone with chronic liver disease that may or may not have been recognised previously [9]. Consistent with the chronic liver failure-sequential organ failure assessment (CLIF-SOFA) renal subscore, a serum creatinine above 1.5 mg/dL was used to indicate renal dysfunction [1,10]. Severity of cirrhosis was graded using the CTP class and the MELD score. All participants were followed for the development of ACLF and for all-cause mortality up to 28 days from enrolment. We first checked continuous variables for normality with the Shapiro-Wilk test; results are reported as numbers and percentages for categorical variables, and since most continuous measures departed from a normal distribution, we used the median (interquartile range) alongside the mean±SD for reference. Group comparisons accordingly relied on the Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables and on the chi-square test or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables, with Fisher's test used whenever an expected cell count fell below five. To identify the plasma cystatin C threshold that best predicted 28-day mortality, we constructed a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and selected the cut-off that maximised the Youden index (sensitivity + specificity − 1); its area under the curve (AUC) was compared with that of the CTP and MELD scores, each computed in the same direction (death as the positive outcome), using DeLong's test. Significance was set at a two-sided p-value below 0.05, and all computations were carried out in SPSS Statistics version 21.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Results A total of 100 patients with acutely decompensated liver cirrhosis, recruited over 18 months, were included in the analysis. The mean (SD) age was 48.8 (10.1) years (median 48.5, range 29-76), with the largest proportion of participants (34%) in the 41-50-year age group; 82 (82%) were men. Alcohol was the commonest aetiology of cirrhosis (75 patients, 75%), followed by hepatitis B (10, 10%), hepatitis E (5, 5%) and hepatitis C (3, 3%); none of the participants was seropositive for HIV. On presentation, ascites was documented in 93 patients (93%), haematemesis/malena in 90 (90%), icterus in 89 (89%), hepatic encephalopathy in 88 (88%), pedal oedema in 64 (64%) and pallor in 61 (61%). Most participants were classified as CTP class C (79%), followed by class B (17%) and class A (4%); the median CTP score was 11 (IQR 10-12). The median MELD score was 34.3 (IQR 32.2-37.1), and 64% of participants had a MELD score of 30-39. Acute-on-chronic liver failure developed in 41 patients (41%), and 44 patients (44%) died within 28 days of enrolment. The overall mean (SD) plasma cystatin C was 3.57 (3.72) mg/L (median 2.16, IQR 1.13-4.03); 77 patients (77%) had a level above 1.11 mg/L. The association between clinical features and 28-day mortality is shown in Table 1. Icterus was significantly more frequent among non-survivors (p=0.021). Other clinical and aetiological features did not differ significantly between those who died and those who survived. Laboratory parameters associated with 28-day mortality were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test, as none were normally distributed (Table 2). Platelet count, blood urea, serum creatinine, plasma cystatin C, and total, direct, and indirect bilirubin were all significantly higher among non-survivors (p<0.05 for all). Plasma cystatin C level did not differ significantly between patients with and without ACLF, either as a continuous variable (mean (SD) 4.31 (4.31) vs 3.05 (3.19) mg/L; p=0.271) or when dichotomised at 1.11 mg/L (83% vs 73% of patients above this cut-off; p=0.240); the strength of association was small (point-biserial r=0.17). In contrast, plasma cystatin C was strongly and significantly higher among patients who died within 28 days than among survivors (mean (SD) 5.49 (4.70) vs 2.06 (1.54) mg/L; median 3.70 vs 1.35 mg/L; Mann-Whitney U=1925, p<0.001), with a large effect size (point-biserial r=0.46). Among the 44 patients who died, 40 (91%) had a cystatin C level above 1.11 mg/L, compared with 37 of 56 survivors (66%; χ2=8.58, p=0.003). On ROC curve analysis, plasma cystatin C predicted 28-day mortality with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.781 (95% CI 0.688-0.874; p<0.001) (Figure 1). A cut-off of ≥2.5 mg/L gave a sensitivity of 73% (95% CI 57-85), specificity of 75% (95% CI 62-86), positive predictive value of 70% (95% CI 54-82), negative predictive value of 78% (95% CI 64-88) and diagnostic accuracy of 74% (95% CI 64-82); the odds ratio for 28-day mortality at this cut-off was 7.15 (95% CI 2.95-17.35). Diagnostic performance of cystatin C, CTP score, and MELD score for predicting 28-day mortality is compared in Table 3 and Figure 2. On DeLong's test, the AUROC for cystatin C was significantly higher than for the CTP score (0.506, 95% CI 0.392-0.620) or MELD score (0.508, 95% CI 0.392-0.624) (p<0.001 for both), while both the CTP and MELD scores did not differ significantly from each other (p=0.898). Discussion In this prospective cohort of 100 patients with acutely decompensated liver cirrhosis, plasma cystatin C was significantly elevated in patients who died within 28 days of admission and discriminated 28-day mortality substantially better than the conventional CTP and MELD scores, with a proposed cut-off of 2.5 mg/L yielding 73% sensitivity and 75% specificity. The cystatin C level, however, did not differ significantly between patients with and without ACLF, suggesting that in this cohort it performed better as a marker of short-term mortality risk than as a discriminator of ACLF itself. The prevalence of ACLF in our cohort (41%) is comparable to that reported in other prospective cohorts of acute decompensation of cirrhosis [7,11]. Our finding that plasma cystatin C rises significantly in patients who die within 28 days corroborates a large multicentre cohort in which baseline cystatin C independently predicted 90-day mortality, renal dysfunction, hepatorenal syndrome and ACLF [7], as well as reports from hepatitis B virus-related ACLF and decompensated cirrhosis in which a higher cystatin C level was associated with increased short-term mortality, and in which combining cystatin C with total bilirubin improved prediction of survival beyond conventional severity scores [11,12]. Cystatin C has similarly been reported to identify acute kidney injury earlier than creatinine and to independently predict outcome in other cohorts of cirrhosis, with proposed cut-offs in a range comparable to ours [13-15]. Unlike some of these reports, we did not find a significant association between cystatin C level and ACLF status itself; this may reflect differences in the criteria used to define ACLF, in disease severity, or in sample size across studies. The limited discrimination we observed for the CTP and MELD scores is in keeping with reports that conventional severity scores can perform inconsistently for short-term mortality prediction across ACLF cohorts and that other markers have sometimes outperformed them [16]. It may also reflect the referral bias of a tertiary-care centre, where nearly four-fifths of our participants were already in CTP class C, narrowing the range over which these scores could discriminate outcome. A few limitations temper these findings. The work was carried out at one tertiary-care centre with no liver-transplant programme, and none of our participants were transplanted during follow-up. This probably contributed to the relatively high mortality we observed and limits how far the results can be extended to centres where transplantation is available. As an observational study, it can establish association but not causation, and our cohort was predominantly male and alcohol-related with a high proportion of CTP class C disease, which may limit generalisability to milder or aetiologically different populations. The sample size, while adequate for the pre-specified diagnostic-accuracy calculations, limited subgroup analysis by aetiology or organ-failure pattern; we also relied on univariable comparisons and ROC analysis rather than multivariable regression, so we cannot exclude confounding by variables such as age or bilirubin, and the proposed cystatin C cut-off requires external, ideally multivariable, validation before clinical use. Strengths include the prospective design, pre-specified sample-size calculation, and head-to-head comparison of cystatin C with two established prognostic scores in the same cohort using the same outcome definition; this is consistent with reports that cystatin C-based measures can add incremental value for the early detection of renal impairment even in milder disease [17]. Conclusions In this cohort, plasma cystatin C measured within 48 hours of admission was associated with a greater risk of death during the subsequent 28 days and showed better mortality discrimination than the CTP or MELD scores. It did not, however, distinguish ACLF status. Confirmation in larger multicentre cohorts is needed before the proposed 2.5 mg/L threshold can be applied clinically. If validated, cystatin C may provide a practical adjunct to established prognostic assessment in acutely decompensated cirrhosis. References - Moreau R, Jalan R, Gines P, et al.: Acute-on-chronic liver failure is a distinct syndrome that develops in patients with acute decompensation of cirrhosis. supplementary_news.content_title: Serum Uric Acid and Disease Severity in Chronic Liver Disease: A Cross-Sectional Study of Its Association With Child-Pugh Class
supplementary_news.content: Abstract Background: Chronic liver disease (CLD) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, with India accounting for the highest absolute number of cirrhosis-related deaths globally. Serum uric acid (SUA), the end product of purine metabolism, is increasingly recognised as a marker of oxidative stress and metabolic derangement and has been reported to be elevated in CLD. The Child-Pugh score remains the most widely used bedside tool for assessing hepatic functional reserve. Data regarding the association of SUA with Child-Pugh class and CLD-related complications in Indian tertiary care settings remain limited. Objectives: The study aimed to estimate SUA levels in patients with CLD at admission, determine their association with disease severity according to Child-Pugh class, and assess their association with CLD-related complications. Methods: This cross-sectional, observational study was conducted over 18 months in the Department of General Medicine at a tertiary care teaching hospital. Ninety-two consecutive patients with CLD aged 18-65 years were enrolled. Fasting SUA, liver function tests, haemogram, and coagulation parameters were recorded, and disease severity was graded using the Child-Pugh classification. Continuous variables were compared using the independent-samples t-test or one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons. Categorical associations were assessed using Pearson's chi-square test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. A two-tailed p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: The mean age was 47.6 years, with a male predominance (76.1%). Alcoholic liver disease was the most common aetiology (65.2%). Sixty-four (69.6%) patients had elevated SUA (>7.2 mg/dL, the cutoff applied uniformly to both sexes), with an overall mean SUA of 7.1 ± 1.9 mg/dL. Mean SUA increased progressively across Child-Pugh classes A (5.2 ± 1.1 mg/dL), B (6.9 ± 1.3 mg/dL), and C (8.4 ± 1.6 mg/dL) (ANOVA F(2,89)=37.38, p<0.001), with all pairwise comparisons significant after Bonferroni correction (all p<0.001). SUA was also significantly associated with Child-Pugh class in categorical analysis (χ2(2)=22.00, p<0.001). Patients with complications had higher mean SUA than those without complications (8.0 ± 1.5 vs. 5.6 ± 1.2 mg/dL; t(90)=8.08, p<0.001), and elevated SUA was significantly associated with any complication (χ2(1)=17.63, p<0.001). Child-Pugh class was similarly associated with complications (χ2(2)=15.68, p<0.001). Among individual complications, elevated SUA was significantly associated with hepatic encephalopathy (χ2(1)=6.15, p=0.013) but not with variceal bleeding, hepatorenal syndrome, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, or portal hypertension (all p>0.05). Conclusion: Hyperuricaemia was common in this CLD cohort and was significantly associated with Child-Pugh class and the overall presence of complications. These findings support a hypothesis-generating association between SUA and disease severity rather than an established prognostic or independent role. Except for hepatic encephalopathy, SUA was not significantly associated with individual complications. Larger prospective multicentric studies adjusting for renal function and other confounders are needed before SUA can be considered a clinical adjunct marker. Introduction Chronic liver disease (CLD) is a progressive pathological process characterised by ongoing hepatocellular destruction and regeneration, culminating in fibrosis and cirrhosis [1]. Liver cirrhosis and other CLDs were responsible for approximately 1.47 million deaths worldwide in 2019, and India recorded the highest absolute number of deaths and disability-adjusted life-years attributable to this disease group of any single country [1]. Within the Asia-Pacific region, alcohol-related liver disease and chronic viral hepatitis B and C remain the dominant aetiologies, with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) emerging as a rapidly growing contributor amid the region's changing dietary and metabolic profile [2]. Uric acid is the terminal product of purine catabolism, generated predominantly in the liver and intestine through the sequential oxidation of hypoxanthine and xanthine by xanthine oxidase. Beyond its traditional association with gout and nephrolithiasis, elevated serum uric acid (SUA) is now recognised as a marker of oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and low-grade systemic inflammation -- mechanisms that are also implicated in metabolic syndrome and progressive hepatic injury [3]. In the setting of CLD, hyperuricaemia has been attributed to a combination of increased purine turnover from hepatocyte necrosis, reduced hepatic and renal clearance of urate as synthetic and excretory function deteriorates, and the metabolic derangements that accompany portal hypertension and diuretic therapy. Population-based data from the United States have shown that an elevated SUA level is independently associated with both the development of cirrhosis and the presence of elevated hepatic transaminases, even after adjustment for established risk factors [4]. A similar mechanistic link between hyperuricaemia and progressive fatty liver disease -- via insulin resistance, hepatic lipogenesis, and inflammasome activation -- has been described in patients with NAFLD [5]. The Child-Pugh score (originally the Child-Turcotte classification [6], later modified by Pugh and colleagues to replace nutritional status with prothrombin time [7]) remains the most widely used bedside tool for grading the severity of hepatic dysfunction and for predicting short- and medium-term survival in patients with cirrhosis. It combines two laboratory variables (serum bilirubin and albumin) with three clinical or coagulation variables (prothrombin time/international normalised ratio (INR), ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy) to stratify patients into Class A, B, or C, corresponding to one-year survival rates of approximately 100%, 81%, and 45%, respectively. Although newer objective scores such as the model for end-stage liver disease (MELD) have gained prominence [8], particularly for transplant allocation, the Child-Pugh score continues to be favoured in routine clinical practice for its simplicity and bedside applicability [9]. Several small, single-centre studies from South Asia have reported a positive association between SUA level and Child-Pugh class, suggesting that SUA could serve as an inexpensive, widely available adjunct to existing severity-scoring systems [10,11]. However, the strength of this association, and its relationship with specific disease complications such as hepatic encephalopathy, variceal bleeding, hepatorenal syndrome, and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, has varied across studies and study populations, and dedicated Indian tertiary care data remain limited. Establishing this relationship more precisely could support the use of SUA as a low-cost tool for early risk stratification, particularly in resource-constrained settings where its estimation is already inexpensive and widely accessible. The present study was therefore undertaken to estimate SUA levels at admission in patients with CLD attending a tertiary care teaching hospital, to determine the association between SUA level and disease severity as graded by the Child-Pugh score, and, as a secondary objective, to study the association between SUA level and CLD-related complications. Materials & Methods Study design and setting This was a hospital-based, cross-sectional, observational study conducted in the Department of General Medicine at NKP Salve Institute of Medical Sciences and Research Center and Lata Mangeshkar Hospital, Nagpur, Maharashtra, India, from May 1, 2024, to October 31, 2025. Patients with a diagnosis of CLD were screened consecutively over a period of 18 consecutive months, as they presented to the department. The study was conducted after obtaining approval from the institutional ethics committee (IEC Reference No. 29/2024; approval date: April 18, 2024), and it was carried out in accordance with the ethical standards of the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and its later amendments. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants before enrolment. Sample size calculation As no comparable prior study had reported an effect size for the primary association between SUA and Child-Pugh class that could be used for a formal a priori power calculation, the sample size was instead estimated using the anticipated proportion of raised SUA among patients with CLD reported in a prior study from a comparable tertiary care setting (anticipated proportion = 40%) [10], as a pragmatic basis for ensuring an adequately sized cohort. Using the standard formula for estimating a single proportion with a fixed absolute precision, where Z1−a is the standard normal deviate corresponding to a two-tailed alpha error of 5% (1.96), p is the anticipated proportion (0.40), and d is the absolute precision (±10%), the calculated minimum sample size was 92. All 92 subjects fulfilling the eligibility criteria during the study period were enrolled by consecutive sampling. This proportion-based justification, rather than a formal power calculation for the primary SUA-Child-Pugh class association, is acknowledged as a limitation of the study design (see Limitations). Participants Patients were enrolled consecutively, as they presented and met the following eligibility criteria. Patients aged 18-65 years of either sex with a clinical, biochemical, and/or imaging-based diagnosis of CLD, who were willing to participate, were included. Patients with a history of malignancy (leukaemia or lymphoma), gout, chronic kidney disease (defined as a pre-existing clinical diagnosis of chronic kidney disease or a documented estimated glomerular filtration rate <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 for >3 months, based on history and available prior records), those on drugs known to affect serum urate (frusemide, thiazide diuretics, allopurinol, or febuxostat), those undergoing chemotherapy, those with recent major surgery or trauma, and those who did not provide informed consent were excluded. Acute kidney injury at presentation was not used as a separate exclusion criterion, other than where it manifested as hepatorenal syndrome, which was captured as a study complication; serial serum creatinine measurements were not systematically available for all participants to permit a formal, protocol-driven assessment of acute kidney injury by standard consensus criteria, and this is discussed further as a limitation. Data collection A detailed history (including age, sex, socio-economic status, and relevant lifestyle factors such as alcohol use) and a thorough clinical examination, including a systemic examination directed at features of CLD, were performed and recorded on a structured case record form for every participant. Relevant risk factors and comorbidities elicited on history and examination were also recorded. Procedure Venous blood samples were drawn after an overnight fast at the time of admission, before the initiation of any drug that could alter SUA level. Complete blood count was estimated on an automated five-part haematology analyser (Siemens Advia 2120). Fasting and post-prandial blood glucose were measured by the glucose oxidase-peroxidase method. Lipid profile was assessed on a Siemens Dimension RxL Max analyser, with total cholesterol measured by the cholesterol oxidase-peroxidase method, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol by a direct (polyethene glycol-modified enzyme) method, and triglycerides by an enzymatic endpoint method. SUA was estimated by the uricase-peroxidase (enzymatic colorimetric) method on the same Siemens Dimension RxL Max autoanalyser. A resting 12-lead electrocardiogram was recorded using a Schiller AT-2 plus machine where clinically indicated. Liver function tests (serum bilirubin, direct and indirect fractions, aspartate and alanine aminotransferases, and serum albumin) and prothrombin time/INR were estimated by standard laboratory methods on the day of admission. Disease severity was graded using the Child-Turcotte-Pugh classification, which assigns 1-3 points each for serum bilirubin, serum albumin, prothrombin time prolongation (or INR), ascites, and grade of hepatic encephalopathy; the summed score classifies patients as Class A (5-6 points), Class B (7-9 points), or Class C (10-15 points) [7]. Presence of complications was recorded on the basis of standard clinical, biochemical, endoscopic, and/or imaging criteria at the time of the index admission, applying published consensus definitions: hepatic encephalopathy was graded clinically using the West Haven criteria [12]; variceal bleed and clinically evident portal hypertension were defined by endoscopic and/or imaging evidence of oesophagogastric varices with or without active or recent bleeding [13]; hepatorenal syndrome was defined using the revised International Club of Ascites-acute kidney injury (ICA-AKI) criteria [14]; and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis was defined as an ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count >250 cells/mm3 in the absence of a secondary source of infection [15]. Data were entered into a password-protected electronic spreadsheet, verified weekly for accuracy, and kept confidential throughout the study. Outcome measures The primary outcome measures were (i) the SUA level at admission, categorised as normal (≤ 7.2 mg/dL) or elevated (> 7.2 mg/dL), and its association with Child-Pugh class (A, B, or C); and (ii) the mean SUA level compared across Child-Pugh classes and between patients with and without complications. A single cutoff of 7.2 mg/dL, corresponding to the upper limit of the standard laboratory reference range in males, was applied uniformly to both sexes for categorisation, consistent with the approach used in the comparable prior studies referenced for sample size estimation and comparison [10,11]; because the standard upper reference limit is lower in females (approximately 6.0 mg/dL), this uniform threshold may under-detect hyperuricaemia in female participants, and this is discussed further as a limitation. The secondary outcome measure was the association between SUA level and the individual complications of CLD (hepatic encephalopathy, variceal bleeding, hepatorenal syndrome, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and portal hypertension). Statistical analysis Data were entered into Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington) and analysed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version 20 (released 2011; IBM Corp., Armonk, New York). Descriptive statistics are presented as mean ± standard deviation for continuous variables and as frequency (percentage) for categorical variables. For continuous outcomes, the independent-samples Student's t-test was used to compare SUA levels between two groups (presence vs. absence of complications), and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with the F-test was used to compare SUA levels across the three Child-Pugh classes; where the omnibus F-test was significant, pairwise comparisons between each pair of classes (A vs. B, A vs. C, B vs. C) were performed using pooled-variance t-tests with Bonferroni correction for three comparisons. For each categorical association, a single primary test was selected a priori based on table dimensions and expected cell counts: the Pearson chi-square test of independence (uncorrected) was used for all contingency tables in which no more than 20% of cells had an expected count of <5. Fisher's exact test was used instead wherever this assumption was violated, as recommended for sparse tables [16]. A two-tailed p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant throughout. Ethical declaration The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee, and all participants provided written informed consent after being explained the purpose, procedures, and potential risks and benefits of participation. Participants were informed of their right to withdraw at any stage without any effect on their clinical care, and confidentiality of all data was maintained throughout the study. Results A total of 92 patients with CLD fulfilling the eligibility criteria were enrolled consecutively over the 18-month study period. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics are summarised in Table 1. The majority of participants were middle-aged, with the highest proportion in the 51-60-year age group (30.4%) and the lowest below 30 years of age (8.7%); the mean age of the cohort was 47.6 years (calculated from grouped data). There was a marked male predominance (76.1%). Alcoholic liver disease was the leading aetiology (65.2%), followed by NAFLD (15.2%), viral hepatitis (10.9%), and cryptogenic cirrhosis (8.7%). On admission, 64 of 92 (69.6%) patients had an elevated SUA level (>7.2 mg/dL), and 70 of 92 (76.1%) patients were classified as Child-Pugh Class B or C, reflecting a cohort weighted towards moderate-to-advanced hepatic dysfunction at presentation. Distribution of complications among study participants has been presented in Table 2. Hepatic encephalopathy was the most frequent complication (32.6%), followed by portal hypertension (28.3%), variceal bleeding (21.7%), hepatorenal syndrome (13.0%), and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (8.7%). Laboratory parameters of study participants has been presented in Table 3. Mean haemoglobin was 10.8 ± 1.9 g/dL, consistent with mild anaemia, and the mean platelet count was at the lower end of the normal range (1.85 ± 0.72 × 105/mm3). Transaminases and bilirubin were elevated, and serum albumin was reduced, in keeping with impaired synthetic and excretory hepatic function. The overall mean SUA level was 7.1 ± 1.9 mg/dL. supplementary_news.content: News Drug Development FDA Manufacturing Deals Business Job Trends Cell and Gene Therapy Cancer Opinions Press Releases All News & Releases Podcasts Events Jobs Companies Hotbeds More Reports Career Advice NextGen: Top Startups to Watch 40 Under 40 Best Places to Work Employer Resources Advertise Advertise Talent Solutions Post Jobs Submit a Press Release Submit an Event SUBSCRIBE Menu SUBSCRIBE Show Search News Drug Development FDA Manufacturing Deals Business Job Trends Cell and Gene Therapy Cancer Opinions Press Releases All News & Releases Podcasts Events Jobs Companies Hotbeds More Reports Career Advice NextGen: Top Startups to Watch 40 Under 40 Best Places to Work Employer Resources Advertise Advertise Talent Solutions Post Jobs Submit a Press Release Submit an Event Search Query Submit Search Press Releases Orca Bio Announces the Publication of TREGZITM Long-Term Overall Survival Data in Transplantation and Cellular Therapy September 17, 2026 | 8 min read Twitter LinkedIn Facebook Email Print Three-year data highlight the long-term results of TREGZI compared to registry post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) in patients with hematologic malignancies MENLO PARK, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Orca Bio, a commercial-stage biotechnology company committed to transforming the lives of patients through high-precision cell therapy, announced the publication of data from a retrospective analysis which suggests a three-year overall survival (OS) benefit with TREGZITM, in patients with hematologic malignancies. This retrospective analysis evaluated data from the Precision-T phase 1b multicenter study comparing TREGZI + tacrolimus (Tac) to a CIBMTR-NMDP registry cohort of patients receiving conventional allo-HSCT + PTCy based GVHD prophylaxis. The findings, featured in the journal Transplantation and Cellular Therapy, showed improved survival outcomes for patients treated with TREGZI compared to similar patients treated with PTCy in the myeloablative setting. The data published in Transplantation and Cellular Therapy reinforce the potential role of high-precision graft engineering platforms and therapeutic interventions like TREGZI, in improving long-term outcomes in patients with blood cancer. “Allogeneic stem cell transplant has long been considered the only curative option for advanced hematologic malignancies, but the risks associated with them – including graft versus host disease (GVHD) – are potentially life threatening,” said Caspian Oliai, MD, medical director of the UCLA Bone Marrow Transplantation Stem Cell Processing Center. “While there are treatment options available to help prevent GVHD, data on the impact of them on overall survival have been limited. The findings from this retrospective analysis on the recently approved therapy, TREGZI, point to the value of cell therapy in potentially improving transplant outcomes for patients without sacrificing long-term survival.” The TREGZI arm was associated with higher OS over a three-year follow-up period compared to PTCy arm (HR=0.41; log-rank p=0.003). Overall survival at one, two, and three years for patients receiving TREGZI (n=76) was 96% (95% CI: 88%-99%), 86% (76%-92%), and 83% (73%-90%), respectively. For patients included in the PTCy cohort (n=360), OS at one, two, and three years was 81% (95% CI:77%-85%), 72% (67%-77%), and 66% (60%-71%), respectively. Historically, a drug cocktail of Tacrolimus/methotrexate (tac/MTX) was the predominant standard of care to prevent GVHD for patients following alloHSCT. However, there has been increased adoption of different approaches to GVHD prevention such as, PTCy-based regimens and the recently approved high-precision cell therapy, TREGZI. In clinical studies, both TREGZI + Tac and allo-HSCT + PTCy have demonstrated the reduced cumulative incidence of GVHD relative to Tac/MTX. “We welcome the publication of these data in Transplantation and Cellular Therapy as it contributes to the body of evidence that supports the therapeutic value of graft engineering approaches in GVHD,” said Nate Fernhoff, co-founder and CEO, Orca Bio. “We are a company committed to redefining what’s possible for patients in allogeneic cell therapy, and these data reinforce the value of Orca Bio’s technology in the durable restoration of a healthy immune system and reducing treatment-related toxicities in patients with blood cancer.” About the Phase 1b Study and Comparative Analysis The data published in Transplantation and Cellular Therapy, were based on a retrospective analysis of long-term survival follow up from a Phase 1b multicenter trial evaluating TREGZI for the treatment of hematologic malignancies, data from which have been presented at multiple scientific congresses including the American Society of Hematology (ASH) and the Tandem meetings of ASTCTTM and CIBMTRTM. The three-year OS outcomes observed with TREGZI were compared to a historical cohort of patients receiving an allogeneic stem cell transplant with PTCy-based GVHD prophylaxis. The cohort included was from registry data collected by CIBMTR-NMDP. The inclusion criteria for this comparative analysis were similar to those of the TREGZI Precision-T Phase 3 trial including: patients who were ≤65 years of age with confirmed diagnoses of either intermediate- or high-risk acute myeloid leukemia (AML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) in complete remission or myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), who were treated with a myeloablative conditioning (MAC) regimen, and an 8/8 HLA-matched donor. IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION AND INDICATION WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS Graft Failure: Graft failure has occurred after TREGZI administration. Screen TREGZI recipients for antidonor antibodies that may prevent engraftment. Monitor patients closely for laboratory evidence of hematopoietic recovery. Graft-Versus-Host Disease: Acute and chronic Graft-Versus-Host disease (GVHD), including life-threatening and fatal cases, occurred following treatment with TREGZI. Acute GVHD manifests as maculopapular rash, gastrointestinal symptoms, and elevated bilirubin. Chronic GVHD may include skin rash, mouth sores, dry eyes, liver inflammation, and development of scar tissue in the skin and joints and damage to the lungs. Treat patients with a single agent calcineurin inhibitor as prophylaxis to decrease the risk of GVHD. Monitor for signs and symptoms of GVHD, and treat if GVHD develops. Infusion Reactions: Infusion reactions (IRs) may occur during or following treatment with TREGZI. Serious hypersensitivity reactions including anaphylaxis may occur to DMSO, human serum albumin (HSA), Dextran or murine protein present in TREGZI. IRs may begin within minutes of the start of TREGZI infusion, although symptoms may continue to intensify and not peak for several hours after the completion of the infusion. Monitor patients for signs and symptoms of IRs during and after TREGZI administration. When a reaction occurs, pause the infusion and institute supportive care as needed. Premedicate patients with antipyretics and histamine antagonists prior to infusion to reduce the incidence and intensity of infusion reactions. Secondary Malignancies and Malignancies of Donor Origin: Secondary malignancies and malignancies of donor origin may occur following treatment with TREGZI. Development of secondary malignancies, including posttransplantation lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) may occur many years after transplantation. PTLD manifests as a lymphoma-like disease favoring non-nodal sites. PTLD is usually fatal if not treated. Serial monitoring of blood for EBV DNA may be warranted in patients with persistent cytopenias. No patient treated with TREGZI has developed PTLD. Monitor for malignancies of donor origin and secondary malignancies. Contact Orca Bio at 1-877-411-6722 if any patient is diagnosed with a secondary malignancy or a malignancy of donor origin. Transmission of Infectious Agents: Transmission of serious infectious or communicable disease or agents may occur with TREGZI treatment as it is derived from human donor blood and manufactured using animal-derived reagents. Risks of transmission of infectious agents may occur despite screening or testing of donors. Risks of transmission of serious infections include, but are not limited to, human immunodeficiency virus, human T cell lymphotropic virus (HTLV)-1 and -2, hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), Treponema pallidum, Trypanosoma cruzi, West Nile virus (WNV), cytomegalovirus, transmissible spongiform encephalopathy agents and vaccinia. Monitor patients for signs and symptoms of infections, perform tests for infectious agents and treat as clinically indicated. ADVERSE REACTIONS The most common adverse reactions (incidence ≥ 20%) were mucositis, diarrhea, rash, viral infections, infections pathogen unspecified, abdominal pain, vomiting, nausea, bacterial infections, hemorrhage, aGVHD, edema, and fungal infections. The most common Grade 3-4 laboratory abnormalities (≥ 20%) are lymphocyte count decreased, platelet count decreased, leukocyte count decreased, neutrophil count decreased and hemoglobin decreased. INDICATIONS AND USAGE TREGZI is indicated for use in matched donor hematopoietic stem cell transplantation with myeloablative preparative regimen, for hematopoietic and immunologic reconstitution and to improve chronic graft-versus-host-free survival, in the treatment of adults with hematological malignancies. Please see accompanying full Prescribing Information. About TREGZITM TREGZITM is the first-and-only FDA approved precision-cell therapy for allogeneic transplant in adults with hematologic malignancies to improve survival free of cGVHD. It is indicated for use in matched donor hematopoietic stem cell transplantation with myeloablative preparative regimen, for hematopoietic and immunologic reconstitution and to improve chronic graft-versus-host-disease-free survival, in the treatment of adults with hematological malignancies. TREGZI is a personalized treatment manufactured for each individual patient using living cells from a matched donor. TREGZI uses hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) to reconstitute the immune system, highly purified regulatory T cells (Tregs) to suppress GVHD and conventional T cells (Tcons) to accelerate immune reconstitution and produce graft-versus-leukemia (GVL) activity. The FDA approval of TREGZI was based on the results of Precision-T, a randomized, open-label, multi-center study that evaluated the safety, efficacy and tolerability of TREGZI compared with conventional allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant (alloHSCT). About Orca Bio Orca Bio is a commercial-stage biotechnology company developing high-precision cell therapies for the treatment of blood cancer and autoimmune diseases. The company’s manufacturing platform uses single-cell precision to create proprietary, uniquely defined products designed to replace a patient’s diseased blood and immune system with a healthy one. At Orca Bio, we are on a mission to redefine what’s possible for patients by transforming the field of curative allogeneic cell therapy. For more information, visit www.orcabio.com. (OTCQB: AVAI) (“Avaí” or the “Company”), an emerging biotechnology company developing transformative cell-based therapies for diabetes, age-related disorders, and anti-aging, today announced, together with its joint venture partner and global biotechnology company Austrianova, the successful completion of comprehensive adventitious agent and viral testing of its GMP Master Cell Bank (MCB), from which its Working Cell Bank (WCB) was recently established. With the testing completed and the WCB now successfully established, Avaí Bio and Austrianova have completed an important milestone in the development of the Company’s genetically modified α-Klotho-producing cell line. The testing confirmed that the MCB, and in turn, the WCB are free of a broad range of potentially contaminating viruses and other adventitious agents. The testing included more than 30 viruses, including significant human and animal pathogens such as human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), human cytomegalovirus (HCMV), and hepatitis B and C viruses. Additional testing confirmed the absence of other potential contaminants, including bacteria, mycoplasma, fungi, and yeast. The testing was conducted by an experienced, accredited third-party laboratory in accordance with applicable industry guidelines, including those established by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The completion of this testing represents an important step in the development and characterization of the Company’s α-Klotho-producing cell line. The cells, which were in-licensed from Klothea Bio, have been genetically modified to overexpress α-Klotho, a protein associated with healthy aging and protection against age-related disease. Klothonova, the joint venture company formed by Avaí Bio and Austrianova, is now focused on further characterization of the Klotho-producing cells and on using the WCB to establish optimal production parameters for the development of the Cell-in-a-Box® encapsulated cell product. “We are pleased to announce the successful completion of this important testing milestone,” said Chris Winter, Chief Executive Officer of Avaí Bio. “The results provide additional confirmation of the safety and quality of our Master and Working Cell Banks and allow us, together with our partner, to advance the next stages of development. We remain focused on progressing toward our goal of developing long-term, safe and effective cell-based therapies for healthy aging and longevity.” Dr. Brian Salmons, Chief Executive Officer of Austrianova, added, “Comprehensive testing of cell banks for viruses and other adventitious agents is an essential component of biomanufacturing and an important prerequisite for advancing cell-based products toward clinical development. We are pleased that the independently conducted testing confirmed that the MCB, and by default, the WCB were negative for all viruses included in the testing panel. With this milestone completed, we are advancing toward the next steps in the development and production of the Cell-in-a-Box® encapsulated clinical product.” This latest milestone follows the joint venture agreement signed in September 2025, which established Klothonova as a Nevada-based company equally owned by Avaí Bio and Austrianova’s affiliate, SG Austria Pte. Ltd. The joint venture was established to develop a sustainable approach to the production and delivery of α-Klotho—often referred to as the “longevity protein,” a key regulatory protein that is well documented for its anti-aging and protective effects on organs—in patients using Cell-in-a-Box® encapsulated cell-based therapies. Uric acid showed a stronger relationship with impaired glucose among people with MASLD. Combined metabolic assessment could help identify people at greater risk of dysglycaemia. IMPAIRED glucose regulation may be substantially more common among people with both metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and hyperuricaemia, according to a study of almost 18,000 adults. Researchers found that having both metabolic conditions was associated with nearly five-times the odds of impaired fasting glucose (IFG), a marker of dysglycaemia that can precede Type 2 diabetes. Identifying Factors Linked to Impaired Glucose Researchers analysed 17,980 adults who underwent health examinations in Jiaozuo, China, during 2025. Participants were assessed for MASLD using ultrasonography and for hyperuricaemia using sex-specific serum uric acid thresholds. They were then categorised according to whether they had neither condition, hyperuricaemia alone, MASLD alone, or both. The researchers investigated how these metabolic abnormalities were associated with IFG, which occurs when fasting blood glucose levels are elevated but do not meet the threshold for diabetes. After adjustment for potential confounding factors, hyperuricaemia alone was associated with approximately twice the odds of IFG compared with having neither condition. MASLD alone was associated with 2.85-times the odds. However, people with both MASLD and hyperuricaemia had 4.82-times the odds of IFG, indicating an additive interaction between the two conditions. Uric Acid May Help Identify Dysglycaemia Risk The relationship between serum uric acid and impaired glucose regulation also differed according to MASLD status. Among people with MASLD, the predicted probability of IFG began increasing more steeply at serum uric acid concentrations of approximately 360 μmol/L. Among those without MASLD, the increase remained more modest until concentrations reached approximately 420 μmol/L. The interaction between MASLD and hyperuricaemia also appeared stronger among women and people without obesity, although further research is required to confirm these subgroup findings. Could Combined Screening Identify Higher-Risk Patients? IFG is an important indicator of abnormal glucose metabolism and can identify people at increased risk of subsequently developing Type 2 diabetes. The findings suggest that considering liver health and serum uric acid alongside conventional glucose measurements could potentially help identify individuals with underlying metabolic dysfunction who may benefit from closer glucose monitoring. However, the study was cross-sectional, meaning it cannot establish whether MASLD or hyperuricaemia causes impaired glucose regulation or increases the subsequent incidence of Type 2 diabetes. The researchers therefore highlight the need for prospective studies to determine whether combined assessment of MASLD and uric acid could improve early identification of people at increased risk of dysglycaemia and Type 2 diabetes. 人体免疫系统就像一支精密的防御部队,细胞因子(如肿瘤坏死因子TNF、白介素IL-6等)和特异性淋巴细胞(如B细胞)是抵御外来细菌、病毒和隐匿病原体的重要哨兵。靶向药物通过精准阻断这些免疫通路来平息体内过度的自身免疫风暴,但这也同时为某些特定病原体的伺机侵袭或体内潜伏感染的死灰复燃打开了缺口。国际多中心登记库(如英国BSRBR、丹麦DANBIO及德国RABBIT)的大数据表明,感染风险的高低并非不可控,它与所选药物的作用靶点、患者的基础体质以及联合用药方案紧密相关。 各类靶向药物的感染风险谱与监测重点对比 不同分子靶点的药物,其诱发的感染类型与危险程度截然不同。了解靶向药物的感染偏好,是实现精准防范的前提: 药物类别 / 代表药物 主要作用机制 高风险感染谱系 核心监测与预防要点 TNF-α抑制剂 阻断肿瘤坏死因子炎症通路 严重细菌性肺炎、败血症、结核病(TB)复燃 用药前必须进行潜伏结核γ-干扰素释放试验(IGRA)排查 CD20单抗 利妥昔单抗(美罗华, Rituxan) 耗竭外周B淋巴细胞,抑制抗体生成 重症细菌感染、乙型肝炎病毒(HBV)再激活 治疗前彻底筛查乙肝五项及HBV-DNA,必要时预防性抗病毒 IL-6受体拮抗剂 托珠单抗(雅美罗, Actemra) 阻断白介素-6介导的级联反应 重症细菌感染、机会性感染,且易掩盖发热等炎症表象 密切随访中性粒细胞计数、血小板及血脂指标,警惕隐匿感染 JAK抑制剂 阻断JAK-STAT胞内信号传导 带状疱疹(水痘-带状疱疹病毒再激活,具剂量依赖性) 治疗启动前优先接种重组带状疱疹疫苗,严密监控神经痛与皮疹 IL-17 / IL-23抑制剂 选择性调控Th17免疫轴 总体严重感染率较低,主要为皮肤黏膜念珠菌感染 加强口腔与皮肤护理,识别真菌感染早期体征,无需常规全员抗真菌筛查 在所有生物制剂中,TNF抑制剂和利妥昔单抗与严重感染、肉芽肿性感染(如活动性结核)复燃的相关性最高;而托珠单抗因其会抑制机体C反应蛋白(CRP)的升高,有时患者即便发生严重细菌感染也不会出现典型高热,容易造成漏诊;使用JAK抑制剂时,带状疱疹的发生率显著攀升,属于临床重点防范场景。 哪些患者属于感染极高危人群? 除药物本身外,患者自身的病生理状态往往决定了感染的严重度。临床研究明确了以下几个最为关键的风险修饰因子: 年龄界限:年龄≥60岁的老年患者,在启动生物制剂治疗后,其感染风险是年轻患者的2.28倍。 伴随慢性疾病:合并慢性阻塞性肺病(COPD)、支气管扩张、糖尿病、慢性肾脏病(CKD)或心血管疾病者,免疫代偿能力显著较弱。 既往感染病史:既往发生过严重肺炎、脓毒症或深部真菌感染的患者,再次用药时的复发风险极高。 激素联用风险(最关键的可逆因素):糖皮质激素是增加感染风险的首要推手。当泼尼松(Prednisone)日剂量达到或超过7.5 mg时,感染风险呈剂量依赖性飙升。若长期高剂量使用泼尼松(剂量≥20 mg/天,且持续超过4周),肺孢子菌肺炎(PJP)的发生率骤增,指南明确建议预防性口服甲氧苄啶(Trimethoprim)–磺胺甲噁唑(Sulfamethoxazole)(复方新诺明)进行阻断。 构建三位一体防御体系:筛查、疫苗与动态监测 令人担忧的是,临床大数据显示,目前仅有15.5%的患者在启动生物治疗前接受了指南推荐的全面基线筛查。这一巨大的认知与执行落差,直接导致了部分可预防感染的发生。构建严密的防御闭环需遵循三大支柱: 第一步:无死角的治疗前基线筛查 在首次用药前,必须完成规范的排查方案:包括潜伏结核筛查(首选γ-干扰素释放试验IGRA与胸部高分辨率CT)、乙型肝炎表面抗原与核心抗体、丙型肝炎抗体、人类免疫缺陷病毒(HIV)筛查以及全血细胞分析。在流行病学特定区域,还需排查类圆线虫等寄生虫隐匿感染。 第二步:抢占先机的疫苗接种时间窗 接种疫苗是赋予机体特异性免疫屏障的核心手段。指南推荐在生物治疗启动前2至6周完成灭活疫苗接种,包括肺炎球菌结合疫苗/多糖疫苗、季节性流感疫苗、乙肝疫苗及重组带状疱疹疫苗(该疫苗为非活疫苗,免疫功能低下者亦可安全接种)。必须牢记:处于重度免疫抑制期内的患者,严禁接种减毒活疫苗。若患者原发病情极其危重、面临不可逆器官损伤风险时,不应为了强行等待疫苗接种而延误靶向治疗时机,应在专科医生权衡下同步推进救治。 第三步:治疗期的规律临床随访 治疗启动后的前4-8周内,应密切复查血常规、肝功能与肾功能,随后每3个月固定复查一次。针对使用托珠单抗的患者,还需额外追踪中性粒细胞绝对值与血脂水平;使用利妥昔单抗者需动态关注免疫球蛋白水平与HBV-DNA滴度。 患者及家属的居家防感染与紧急警报 规范的医学管理需要高效的家庭照护协同配合。患者居家期间应养成科学卫生习惯:保持居室通风、进出公共场所规范佩戴口罩、注意手部清洁、生熟食物分开且彻底煮熟、避免接触活动性感染期人群。一旦出现以下“警报信号”,切勿擅自服用退烧药掩盖病情,应立即就医排查: 体温异常升高(≥38.0°C)或伴随剧烈寒战(使用托珠单抗等抗IL-6药物者,即使体温轻微上升亦不可掉以轻心); 持续加重的咳嗽、咳痰、胸闷、呼吸急促或活动后气喘; 沿身体单侧神经节分布的局部灼痛、刺痛,随后出现的集簇性疱疹(警惕带状疱疹); 排尿灼痛、尿频急、腹泻腹痛或伴随神志淡漠、极度乏力等疑似菌血症表现。 用药前沿探索与MedFind全方位支持 靶向生物治疗并不是一把需要因噎废食的“双刃剑”。临床实践证明,通过系统化筛查与科学预防,绝大多数感染风险都可以被降至最低,患者能够安全地享有前沿生物药带来的疾病缓解,并显著减少长期依赖大剂量激素所产生的严重弊端。为了帮助广大患者攻克重疾治疗过程中的信息壁垒与用药难题,MedFind持续提供专业服务:不仅为您汇聚全球前沿诊疗共识与药物资讯,还提供由资深医学团队支持的AI辅助问诊服务,协助您全面解读病历、评估治疗风险并优化随访方案;同时,依托覆盖全球的合规供应链体系,MedFind开辟了抗癌及重疾药物的跨境直邮渠道,保障急需海外先进治疗方案的患者能够合法、快捷、安心地用上原研好药,构筑属于您的全病程健康守护之盾。 【参考文献】 Microorganisms.
